sentences.text: Teleosaurus was an extinct genus of thalattosuchian reptiles, distant relatives of modern crocodiles adapted to ocean life, that lived during the Middle Jurassic in Europe.
Estimates of its size vary, with some sources stating it was approximately 3 meters in length, while others suggest it measured just over 4 meters.
It possessed a long, slender body and a hydrodynamic shape designed for efficient movement through the water.
Unlike its armored ancestors, Teleosaurus lost its heavy bony armor, developing smooth, slippery skin, palmated feet resembling flippers, and a tail that became thinner and longer, resembling a fin.
It had remarkably short forelimbs that were likely held close to the body while swimming to improve streamlining.
Its mouth contained several rows of needle-like teeth specifically used to catch slippery fish and squid.
Teleosaurus had eyes positioned on the top of its head, allowing it to see above the water while remaining submerged.
Like aquatic turtles, Teleosaurus only went to shore to lay eggs.
Marine crocodiles like Teleosaurus likely incubated eggs internally, with hatchlings emerging fully formed and ready to swim, breathe, and eat.

A 2019 review of Teleosauroidea taxonomy concluded that T. cadomensis is the only valid species, as most other species previously assigned to Teleosaurus were absorbed into T. cadomensis or other genera.
It is debated whether T. geoffroyi is a valid species or a synonym of T. cadomensis, with recent studies favoring synonymy.
